title: A Los Angeles resident’s starting point for city service requests
deck: MyLA311 connects residents with city services, including online requests at any hour.
content_html:
An overflowing bin or a neighborhood maintenance problem can leave Los Angeles residents with a basic question: which city office should receive the report? The city’s MyLA311 service provides a starting point for requesting help and finding the appropriate service.

According to the city’s guidance, residents can submit requests online around the clock. The request type determines where it goes, so choosing the category that matches the issue matters. The Los Angeles Department of Transportation also directs residents to 311 and its online service-request channels.

For a broken or missing sanitation bin, LA Sanitation & Environment directs residents to the Request Service option in the MyLA311 app. That provides a specific route for a common household problem.

Before filing, have the location and a clear description ready. Check the city’s current instructions for the service you need; submitting a request does not establish a guaranteed completion time.

title: San Diego’s Get It Done portal puts neighborhood reports in one place
deck: Residents can report problems ranging from potholes to missed trash collection through the city’s service portal.
content_html:
San Diego residents do not need to guess which department handles every routine neighborhood problem. The city’s Get It Done website organizes service requests by issue, offering a common entry point for reports about streets, sidewalks, waste and other public spaces.

The listed categories include potholes, streetlight problems, graffiti, illegal dumping and missed trash collection. Selecting the matching category helps direct the report. The portal also provides a way to view reports, useful when checking whether a concern has already been logged.

On the mobile app, the city explains how residents can add a photo and identify the location on a map. A precise location and a short description make the problem easier to identify.

This is a route for routine service requests. The city directs emergencies to 911 and lists separate telephone contacts for urgent concerns on the Get It Done page.

Source: City of San Diego. Prepared with AI assistance from the linked public guidance.

title: San Jose 311 lets residents report a problem and follow the request
deck: The city’s website and app cover potholes, graffiti, streetlights and other neighborhood concerns.
content_html:
San Jose’s 311 service gives residents a way to file and track requests without first identifying an individual city employee. The city says requests submitted through its website or mobile app reach the relevant service team for review and an outcome update.

The service includes potholes, graffiti, illegal dumping, abandoned-vehicle concerns and streetlight outages. Residents who do not use a smartphone can begin through the city’s website instead.

Not every issue belongs in the same queue. The city’s Report Issues directory distinguishes 311 requests from other concerns, including private-property code issues and certain transportation problems. Checking that directory first can help identify the right channel.

Use the current service page to check availability and describe the issue clearly. A report starts the city’s review process; it does not promise a particular repair date or outcome.

Source: City of San José. Prepared with AI assistance from the linked public guidance.

title: Not sure which San Francisco office to call? Start with 311
deck: The city’s information line offers round-the-clock help for nonemergency questions and services.
source_name: City and County of San Francisco
content_html:
Finding the right government office can be the first obstacle to getting a simple question answered. San Francisco’s 311 line is designed as a starting point for nonemergency city information and services, including questions that do not fit neatly into a single department.

The city says the service operates every day, 24 hours a day, with assistance in more than 160 languages. Call 311 from within San Francisco, or 415-701-2311 from outside the city. The city also lists 711 for callers who need TDD/TTY access.

Examples of questions the service can help with include public transportation and Muni directions, public records, property assessments and how to reach offices responsible for vital records or other filings.

The practical value is navigation: a resident who does not know which office handles a request can start with 311. Because the line is for nonemergency city matters, it should not replace an emergency call.

Source: City and County of San Francisco. Prepared with AI assistance from the linked public guidance.

title: Fresno’s FresGO and 311 connect residents with neighborhood services
deck: The city offers app, web and phone routes for reporting routine maintenance concerns.
content_html:
Fresno residents have several ways to report a neighborhood problem through the city’s 311 service. Its FresGO app supports reports about graffiti, illegal dumping, potholes, sidewalks, landscaping, water, sewer, waste and parking concerns.

The city describes 311 as a connection between residents and city departments for nonemergency communication. Alongside the app, its website provides a service-request option, telephone information and web chat. Residents can choose the channel that works for them rather than relying on a smartphone alone.

For a streetlight problem, the city asks for the nearest address or the pole number so crews can identify the correct light. That is a useful reminder to gather location details before submitting any maintenance report.

The city lists 311 and 559-621-CITY (2489) as contact numbers. Check the current page for staffing hours and instructions for the issue you are reporting. Immediate threats and life-threatening emergencies belong with 911.

Source: City of Fresno. Prepared with AI assistance from the linked public guidance.

title: Total sugars and added sugars: how to read the two lines on a food label
deck: The FDA’s label guidance explains why the added-sugars number is already part of the total.
content_html:
The two sugar lines on a Nutrition Facts label are not two amounts to add together. According to the FDA, total sugars include both naturally occurring sugars and any added sugars in the product. The added-sugars line identifies the portion included in that total.

Naturally occurring sugars include those in milk and fruit. Added sugars include sugars introduced during processing, as well as sweeteners such as honey and syrups. The distinction lets shoppers compare products beyond a single total-sugar figure.

The percent Daily Value provides another reference point. The FDA describes 5 percent or less as low in added sugars and 20 percent or more as high. Its Daily Value is 50 grams based on a 2,000-calorie diet; that is a labeling reference, not a personalized eating plan.

Read the serving information and the rest of the label as well. The FDA emphasizes that added sugars are only one part of the information available for making food choices.

Source: U.S. Food and Drug Administration. Prepared with AI assistance from the linked public guidance.

title: Clear requests and respectful boundaries belong in everyday relationships
deck: NIH guidance highlights honest conversation, listening and limits as parts of supportive connections.
content_html:
A supportive relationship leaves room for both people to say what they need. The National Institutes of Health’s Social Wellness Toolkit identifies honest expression, listening and respectful disagreement as practical parts of healthy connections with others.

Its guidance encourages people to ask for what they need and listen without blame or judgment. Disagreement should stay focused on the issue rather than becoming a personal attack. Looking for a workable agreement does not require pretending that a difference of opinion has disappeared.

Boundaries belong in that conversation, too. NIH advises deciding what you are and are not willing to do, and recognizing that it is acceptable to say no. Respect and honesty should work in both directions.

The toolkit also distinguishes healthy relationships from abusive ones. Communication advice is not a reason to tolerate violence or coercion. NIH links to additional resources for recognizing that difference and protecting yourself.

Source: National Institutes of Health. Prepared with AI assistance from the linked public guidance.
